tier_reason: README Performance tables show 175x/351x (L2) and 69x/143x (DRAM) vs the CPU Partitioned Cuckoo Filter plus the GQF/TCF numbers exactly as claimed; the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/cuckoo_vs_partitioned.cu, benchmarks/load_factor_benchmark.cu), flags are in meson.build (optimization=3, C++20, sm_80/90/120 gencode; PCF built as a CMake Release subproject), and the arXiv paper states the CUDA versions (13.0 on GH200, 12.9 on RTX PRO 6000) and CPU models (Grace Neoverse V2, Xeon W9-3595X, EPYC 7713P).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.0 (GH200 system) / CUDA 12.9 (RTX PRO 6000 system) per the paper; meson.build defaults optimization=3, cpp_std=c++20, cuda_args -std=c++20 --expt-extended-lambda --expt-relaxed-constexpr -gencode sm_80/sm_90/sm_120; PCF baseline built as a CMake subproject with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; the host C++ compiler version is not stated
corrections.hardware: README tables: NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper (72 ARM Neoverse V2 cores, H100 with 96 GB HBM3 at 3.4 TB/s, Ubuntu 24.04.3, CUDA 13.0); CPU PCF baseline on an Intel Xeon W9-3595X (60 cores / 120 threads, 256 GB DDR5, AlmaLinux 10.1). The paper also evaluates an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB GDDR7, 1.8 TB/s) hosted by an AMD EPYC 7713P (CUDA 12.9).
corrections.caveats: Companion code for arXiv:2603.15486 (v1 2026-03-16; Dortmann, Vieth, Schmidt, JGU Mainz; the id resolves), with DOI 10.1145/3832810.3832822 resolving to the ACM DL. The CPU baseline is the partitioned cuckoo filter of Schmidt et al. (VLDB 2021, tum-db/partitioned-filters) at 120 threads, not the original Fan et al. cuckoofilter. The CPU-vs-GPU speedups mix hardware (GH200 vs Xeon W9-3595X), so much of the 69-351x comes from the platform jump rather than the algorithm alone. Against the append-only GPU Blocked Bloom filter (cuCollections) it is slower: 0.35x insert (L2) and 0.7x insert / 0.9x query (DRAM).

notes: The arXiv id is valid and its abstract matches the README: up to 378x/6x/258x insert/query/delete vs GQF, 4.1x/34.7x/107x vs TCF, and up to 350x vs the fastest multi-threaded CPU cuckoo filter, measured on GH200 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. Tier A is kept, with one gap: the host gcc/clang version is unstated, but nvcc versions and build flags are explicit.

tier_reason: The paper (arXiv:1910.09131, later published at NeurIPS 2020 under an expanded title) compares against a standard Bloom filter, LBF and sandwiched LBF on the malicious-URL and malware datasets, and the 81%/84%, 0.35%-FPR 500Kb-to-300Kb and >80% numbers all appear in it. This is a peer-reviewed FPR/memory comparison with Python code and no hardware or systems methodology, so it is B, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper: Ada-BF/disjoint Ada-BF 'reduce the FPR by over 80% and save 50% of the memory usage over existing learned Bloom filters'. On malicious URLs at a 500Kb filter size, Ada-BF cuts FPR by 81% vs LBF/sandwiched LBF (disjoint Ada-BF: 84%); at FPR ~0.35% the memory drops from over 500Kb (LBF) to 300Kb (over 40% savings). On malware MD5, 0.2% FPR needs ~300Kb for LBF vs 150Kb for Ada-BF (50%), and all learned BFs cut FPR by over 98% vs the standard Bloom filter.
corrections.caveats: Reference Python research code with no LICENSE file (reference/study-only). Peer-reviewed at NeurIPS 2020 as 'Adaptive Learned Bloom Filter (Ada-BF): Efficient Utilization of the Classifier with Application to Real-Time Information Filtering on the Web'. This is a numerical FPR-vs-memory comparison, not a speed benchmark: most headline gains are vs other learned Bloom filters, and the standard BF's bit budget is credited with the classifier size (146Kb on URLs). No CPU/compiler details apply. The repo also ships a PLBF.py baseline.

notes: Numbers are verified on the arXiv PDF. 'Save over 50% memory' is corrected to the paper's 'save 50%'. The last commit was 2022-05-24 (over 4 years ago), so the status is abandoned; there is no license (spdx null, no LICENSE file), so usability stays reference.

tier_reason: The 13%/23%/44% storage-overhead figures appear in the abstract of arXiv:2201.01174, but that paper measures the FastFilter reference code. binfuse's own benchmark (bench/large.cpp, README) reports absolute ns/key for binfuse only, with no Bloom/xor/cuckoo or other baseline. The B tier is inherited from the paper about the vendored xor_singleheader code, not binfuse's own evidence.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (arXiv:2201.01174): binary fuse filters are within 13% of the storage lower bound vs 23% for xor and 44% for Bloom filters, without sacrificing query speed. binfuse's own README bench (sharded_filter, 100M keys only) is absolute with no baseline: populate 48.7-93.5 ns/key, query 46.1-52.6 ns/key. A 10B-key run shows query 150.7 ns (f8) and 682612.8 ns (f16, a 22GB file on a 16GB-RAM machine). No 1B-key results are shown.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: README build uses cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release (CI: gcc-13 / clang-18 on Ubuntu 24.04, FreeBSD clang-18.1, MSYS2); the bench (-DBINFUSE_BENCH=ON, bench/large.cpp) run's compiler/flags are not stated
corrections.hardware: Not stated for the 100M-key runs; the 10B-key run was on an unnamed 16GB-RAM machine (no CPU model)
corrections.caveats: Not a distinct filter implementation: include/binfuse/filter.hpp includes binaryfusefilter.h from the vendored ext/xor_singleheader submodule (FastFilter/xor_singleheader) and calls binary_fuse8/16_allocate/populate/contain directly. binfuse adds a C++20 wrapper, mmap-based (de)serialization via mio, and an MSB-prefix sharded on-disk filter. Its own benchmark has no baseline comparison, and the 13%/23%/44% figures are from the original paper about the upstream code.

notes: Rejected as known-project: the filter core is the already-catalogued FastFilter/xor_singleheader, vendored as a git submodule and called verbatim. binfuse's own contribution (mmap persistence plus sharding for 10B+ keys) has only absolute timings, no head-to-head numbers. If the orchestrator wants it, it fits as a usability/packaging note on the xor_singleheader entry, not as a separate faster-than-baseline row.
